hops.afterHeading: What a growth cone can read
hops.title: Adult central neurons have not forgotten how to grow
hops.text: It is easy to assume that an injured adult spinal cord fails to heal because its neurons can no longer grow axons. In 1981, Samuel David and Albert Aguayo tested that in adult rats. They laid a strip of peripheral nerve as a bridge between the medulla and the spinal cord. Central axons from both ends grew about thirty millimeters into it. The neurons still knew how to grow. Mature neurons grow less readily than young ones, but a big part of what stops them is what their growth cones read at home: cues in adult central myelin, and parts of the scar around an injury, can hold regrowth back.

sources.citation: David S, Aguayo AJ. Axonal elongation into peripheral nervous system "bridges" after central nervous system injury in adult rats. Science. 1981;214(4523):931-933.
Yiu G, He Z. Glial inhibition of CNS axon regeneration. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. 2006;7(8):617-627.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white lab rat sits on a sunny lab bench next to an old light microscope and a stack of glass slides.
image.caption: Given a peripheral nerve bridge, adult central neurons regrew axons; cues in central tissue help explain why they usually don't.

hops.title: Why a meal can make one eye water
hops.text: For some people recovering from a facial nerve injury, such as Bell's palsy, a meal can make one eye water along with the mouth. This is crocodile tears syndrome, named for the old belief that crocodiles weep after killing their prey; the Russian neuropathologist F. A. Bogorad described it. The facial nerve carries autonomic fibers to the salivary glands and to the tear gland. The leading explanation: as damaged fibers regrow, some bound for the salivary glands take the tear-gland route instead. Then eating, chewing or the smell of food can bring tears to one eye. A fiber that regrows along the wrong route can signal the wrong gland.

sources.citation: Tripathy K, Arsiwalla T. Crocodile Tears Syndrome. StatPearls. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing; updated 2025.
Bogorad FA. The symptom of crocodile tears. Introduction and translation by Austin Seckersen. Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences. 1979;34(1):74-79.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A green toy crocodile on a cafe table next to a bowl of soup, a spoon and a folded white handkerchief.
image.caption: The leading explanation: regrowing salivary fibers wander into the tear-gland route, so a meal can bring tears to one eye.

hops.title: Touch your fingertips with one eye closed
hops.text: Hold both index fingers out wide at arm's length, close one eye, and slowly sweep the tips together. Many people miss by a bit; with both eyes open, the tips meet easily. That two-eyed advantage starts at a choice point behind your eyes, the optic chiasm, where each retinal axon either crosses to the other side of the brain or stays put. In mice, only three to five percent stay, and many of those turn away from ephrin-B2 at the midline because they carry its receptor. In primates, roughly half stay, so each side of the brain hears from both eyes about the same spot.

sources.citation: Erskine L, Herrera E. Connecting the retina to the brain. ASN Neuro. 2014;6(6):1759091414562107.
Williams SE, Mann F, Erskine L, et al. Ephrin-B2 and EphB1 mediate retinal axon divergence at the optic chiasm. Neuron. 2003;39(6):919-935.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student at a desk with one eye shut, holding both index fingertips out in front of her with a small gap between them.
image.caption: Fingertips meet more easily with two eyes; that advantage starts where retinal axons choose sides at the optic chiasm.

audio.title: Giraffe detours, cross-eyed cats, and itchy sweaters
audio.transcript:
Once you know that a growing axon reads only what sits within its reach, a few strange corners of the animal kingdom start to make sense.

Start with a giraffe. Its voice box sits just below its skull, so you might expect the nerve that serves it to take a short hop. Instead, its fibers run all the way down the neck inside the vagus nerve. Near the heart they branch off as the recurrent laryngeal nerve, loop under a great artery, and climb all the way back up to the voice box. In the tallest giraffes, whose necks reach about two point four meters, the whole route approaches five meters. The anatomist Richard Owen described it in a giraffe back in eighteen forty-one. Why such a long commute? Because the nerve forms early, when the embryo is tiny and the heart sits near the future throat. It forms just behind the embryonic aortic arches, the vessels that become the great arteries. Later, as the neck lengthens and the heart settles into the chest, the already-connected nerve simply gets dragged along. As with this lesson's pioneers, the route is laid while distances are short. In the giraffe, the fibers already in place then lengthen as the neck grows. The paleontologist Mathew Wedel worked out what this would mean for the long-necked dinosaur Supersaurus, whose neck he estimated at fourteen meters or more. If its nerve took the same detour, single neurons in it probably ran past twenty-eight meters. Some slow, unmyelinated fibers in the vagus conduct as slowly as half a meter per second. If Supersaurus had fibers like those, a slow ache from its voice box could have taken almost a full minute to reach its brain.

Our second story is a Siamese cat. Siamese cats are famous for crossed eyes, and their visual wiring differs from other cats'. In mammals with forward-facing eyes, many retinal axons cross to the opposite side of the brain at a choice point called the optic chiasm, while others, from the outer part of each retina, stay on the same side. That split lets each side of the brain compare the two eyes. In Siamese cats, an inherited mutation sends fibers covering roughly the first twenty degrees of that same-side view across to the wrong side of the brain. In nineteen seventy-three, Ray Guillery and Jon Kaas examined the brain of one white tiger. White tigers inherit a reduction in pigment, and this tiger's visual pathway showed an abnormality like the ones known in albino animals of many species. The authors noted a close link between less pigment, the miswired pathway and crossed eyes.

Finally, guidance cues do not retire when the embryo is finished. A wool sweater that feels fine on healthy skin can set off itching on skin with eczema. In your outer layer of skin, nerve growth factor, which encourages sensory fibers to grow in, is thought to be balanced against Sema three A, the secreted repellent in this lesson's table of cues. In atopic dermatitis, a common kind of eczema, researchers have found less Sema three A in the outer layer of the skin along with more nerve fibers there, which may help make it more sensitive to itch. In one mouse model of eczema, a Sema three A ointment reduced the extra nerve fibers in the skin and cut down on scratching.

A neck that grew after the nerve was laid, a mutation that changes which fibers cross, a repellent that keeps skin nerves in check: three reminders that where an axon ends up depends on its timing and its surroundings.
